entry.title: 🔁 Throwback Thursday: The Time I Abstracted Too Soon
entry.summary:
I still remember this one clearly.
I was working on a feature that needed two slightly different components. Naturally, I thought: “Hmm… let’s be smart and make a reusable abstraction up front.” So I spent a few extra hours generalizing the logic, creating a “flexible” component that could handle any edge case I might encounter in the future. It had flags. It had configuration. It had callbacks.
It was... beautifully abstracted.
A week later, requirements changed. The two components diverged. The flags grew. The logic tangled.
Suddenly, I was maintaining a monster that tried to do everything—and pleased no one. Instead of helping, my abstraction slowed me down. I ended up deleting the whole thing and rewriting each component separately. They were simpler. Easier to test. Easier to reason about. Don't abstract until you have at least 3 real use cases. Premature abstraction feels like a smart move—but often, it’s just guessing in the dark.
What looks “clean” today can turn into tech debt tomorrow.
I copy-paste more in the beginning (yep, you read that right). I wait until duplication hurts before abstracting. I treat abstraction as a response to repetition, not a prediction. Sometimes "Don't Repeat Yourself" needs to take a backseat to "Keep It Simple". If you’ve ever built a generic framework for a problem that never scaled—hey, I’ve been there. And I promise, you're not alone. 😅
